prompt: In the lesson's run without a key, why was the card charged twice?

choices.text: The person tapped Buy twice

choices.text: The server charges every purchase twice by design, once to check the card and once to take the money
choices.why: It appends one purchase per request.

choices.text: The answer was lost and the retry charged again
choices.why: Right. The server had no way to know it was a retry.

choices.text: The timeout was too short for a payment to finish
choices.why: The answer was not slow; it was destroyed.

prompt: Which line describes an idempotent operation?

choices.text: Doing it twice has the effect of doing it once
choices.why: Right. The key makes a POST behave that way.

choices.text: One the server answers in less than a second
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: One sent with POST
choices.why: POST is the method that is not idempotent by definition.

choices.text: One that does not fail
choices.why: Failing has nothing to do with it.

prompt: How does the course describe *The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field*?

choices.text: A browser feature
choices.why: It is a contract between client and server, not a browser behaviour.

choices.text: Part of HTTP since 1999
choices.why: It is recent and still a draft.

choices.text: A header private to Stripe's API
choices.why: Stripe uses it, many APIs copied it, and the IETF drafted it.

choices.text: An IETF draft, not yet an RFC
choices.why: Right, and it is cited as one.

prompt: Where does `buy.ts` call `randomUUID()`, and why there?

choices.text: Inside the loop, so each try is fresh
choices.why: A fresh key per try makes the server see a new purchase.

choices.text: Before the loop, once
choices.why: Right, so every retry carries it. The key names the operation, not the request.

choices.text: On the server, when the purchase is charged
choices.why: Only the device knows a retry is a retry.

choices.text: It hashes the body instead, so equal purchases share a key
choices.why: Two equal purchases may both be wanted.

prompt: A create was sent once and its answer lost. Compaction then folds an update into it and the drain resends under the same key. What happens on the lesson's server?

choices.text: The server applies the update
choices.why: The body differs from the one saved under that key.

choices.text: It is refused with 422, since the key was used with another body
choices.why: Right, which is why a tried operation is never folded into.

choices.text: A second session is created
choices.why: The key exists; the server will not do the work again.

choices.text: The old answer comes back and nothing is wrong
choices.why: That is the server that does not compare bodies, and the update is lost there.

choices.text: SQLite makes UUIDs faster

prompt: Why does the server compare a fingerprint of the body and not only the key?

choices.text: Or a reused key gets the wrong purchase back
choices.why: Right. The guitar request would hear that Statistics was bought.

choices.text: To check the body for viruses before the purchase is charged

prompt: A phone holds a purchase in its outbox for two days and retries it on a server that keeps keys for 24 hours. What happens?

choices.text: The server replays the saved answer
choices.why: It no longer has one.

choices.text: The server refuses with 422
choices.why: It does not remember the key at all.

choices.text: The key looks new and the card is charged again
choices.why: Right. The window must outlast the outbox.

choices.text: The phone refuses to send a key older than a day
choices.why: Nothing on the phone checks the key's age.

prompt: Unlike most 4xx answers, why is the 409 worth retrying?

choices.text: In a moment the key holds a finished answer, and the retry gets it
choices.why: Right. The race ends; the answer stays.

choices.text: 409 is a server error, like a 503, so lesson 9's rule applies to it as well
choices.why: It is a 4xx; the reason it is retried is particular.

choices.text: The first request failed, and the key was released for any other try to use
choices.why: It succeeded, a second later.

choices.text: The key is deleted after a 409
choices.why: It is kept and filled in.

prompt: How many hours does the lesson's server keep an answer under its key?
Which HTTP methods are defined as idempotent?

choices.text: POST and PUT
choices.why: POST is not.

choices.text: POST and DELETE
choices.why: POST is not.

choices.text: PUT and DELETE
choices.why: Right, and the server's code has to keep that promise.

choices.text: GET alone
choices.why: GET is safe and idempotent, but PUT and DELETE are idempotent too.

prompt: After two identical `PUT /sessions/s7`, how many sessions did the server hold?

choices.text: Two, one per request
choices.why: The path names the row, so the second wrote over the first.

choices.text: One
choices.why: Right. The same bytes over themselves.

choices.text: Zero: the second PUT cancelled the first one
choices.why: A PUT stores; it does not cancel.

choices.text: It refused the second with 409
choices.why: There is no key and nothing to refuse.

prompt: Which of these still need an idempotency key even with a client-made id? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: a PUT that also sends a confirmation e-mail
choices.why: Its row is idempotent; its side effect is not.

choices.text: charging a card for a course
choices.why: The effect is at the processor.

choices.text: adding 25 minutes to the week's total
choices.why: An increment, said twice, adds twice.

choices.text: storing session s7 as 25 minutes of guitar
choices.why: That states the whole result; PUT is enough.

prompt: A team adds keys but makes a new one each time the drain retries. Lesson 9's `drop` happens. What does the server do?

choices.text: Replays the first answer
choices.why: The retry carries a key it has never seen.

choices.text: Refuses the retry with 422
choices.why: A new key is not a reused key.

choices.text: Answers 409, since two keys for one purchase arrive close together
choices.why: They arrive one after the other, and they differ.

choices.text: Does the work again, as if there were no key
choices.why: Right. A key per request is no key at all.
